source.title: A Large Scale Investigation of Scaling Limits in Chemical Language Models
source.authors: Roshan Balaji; Kamran Chitsaz; Quentin Fournier; N. Bhatt; S. Chandar

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports SAE feature-property association measures in chemical language models, but does not test whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, whether apparent mixtures share a feature, or the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures SAE feature monosemanticity as the largest absolute correlation with evaluated molecular properties. That is related to interpretability, but it does not measure individual neurons’ responses to unrelated kinds of input or vary the activation range or explanation-scoring method. The results below are recorded as related findings that fit none of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper is a scaling study of chemical language models. Its only interpretability results are SAE 'monosemanticity', defined as the mean over live SAE features of the largest absolute Pearson correlation with 36 molecular properties, plus a probe comparison of SAE latents against residual-stream neurons for functional groups. Neither result measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Neither tests superposition, capacity, architecture effects on a polysemantic share, or measurement dependence of neuron polysemanticity. The authors themselves say the measures indicate alignment with properties rather than single-concept encoding.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report rising SAE feature-property associations during training and with scale. They caution that these indicate alignment with the evaluated properties rather than single-concept encoding. They also report a modest SAE-latent advantage over neurons for functional-group probes. The paper's main conclusion concerns goal-directed generation saturating near 5M parameters despite better loss and representations.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies chemical language models with layer-wise linear probes and sparse autoencoders; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization method.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE monosemanticity varies qualitatively with layer and training progress: the early-layer measure rises, while middle- and late-layer measures peak mid-training and then decline slightly.

fits_no_version.finding: In the 32M chemical LM, SAE features' max property correlation and the fraction of property-associated features (>0.4) increase over training, with layer-dependent trends.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature-property alignment in chemical language models grows with training and depends on layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes on middle-layer SAE latents beat probes on residual-stream neurons for 7 of 10 functional groups, by up to 0.034 F1. Where neurons win, the margin is at most 0.003 (Table D2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents make functional-group concepts slightly more linearly accessible than residual-stream neuron bases in chemical LMs.

record.code_released: The authors state that they will release code and model artifacts; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The results concern SAE features in chemical language models, not individual neurons tested on unrelated input types. The SAE metric is a correlation with a limited set of evaluated molecular properties, and several reported layer/training trends have no numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text.

untested.parts: No measure of the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts in transformer LMs. Residual-stream neurons appear only as a probe baseline.
No test of superposition or capacity as cause. The 16x SAE dictionary is used as a tool.
No comparison of polysemantic neuron share across activation functions or architectures.
Not addressed. The metric choice is fixed and not varied.

record.verdict_notes: The interpretability results concern SAE features and residual-stream neurons, not MLP neurons. No result bears on any version, and no verdict labels are given. Table D2 (SAE vs neuron probe F1) is not recorded as a row, but it also fits no version.

versions.untested_parts: Vision models and neuron responses to image inputs.
Polysemanticity rates in language models responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether superposition or capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Changes in the share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization, and the associated performance cost.
Whether apparently polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs, or whether unrelated mixtures are rare.
Whether polysemanticity depends on the activation range examined or on explanation-scoring choices.
